..
Issued at 356 AM CDT Tue Sep 8 2026

Change is afoot ... but the change that most probably want is still 
a day away. Instead, today will be highlighted by a brief resurgence 
of heat across much of the area. As the remnant Omega Block that 
helped yield the prolonged heat continues to break down, the mid-
level low lifting into the Canadian Plains will push the mid-
level/500mb ridge back overhead and with it the 850mb thermal ridge. 
Additionally, winds will shift back more southerly, helping lift a 
plume of moisture/higher dew points into the area.  All of that will 
yield highs jumping back into the mid 90s to around 100 and heat 
index values toward 105 or greater in many locations. Given some 
displacement between highest temps and highest dew points, this 
tends to result in similar forecast heat index values for a majority 
of the CWA. The exception may be the far NE, such as Kirksville, 
where both peak heat and peak humidity may not quite make it. This 
also results in both continued and renewed heat headlines. SW areas, 
including the KC Metro counties, remain in an Extreme Heat Warning 
given the prolonged duration they have experienced. Areas to the 
N/NE/E, to a line from roughly Bethany to Columbia, will have a Heat 
Advisory in place. At this time, all heat headlines expire this 
evening, but there remains the potential for far southern counties 
of the CWA to be extended into Wednesday, all dependent on frontal 
progression. Fairly significant uncertainty remains in that regard, 
as seen in NBM probabilities of MaxT >= 95 and LREF probabilities of 
ApparentT > 100 on Wednesday. In both cases, both struggle to depict 
probabilities > 70 percent. Collaboration with SGF/LSX yielded the 
decision to hold off on Wednesday at this time, as hinted above. The 
noted trend within NBM and LREF probabilities has been a tad slower 
frontal progression, reflected in bit higher probabilities vs 24 hrs 
ago. 

As the aforementioned front drops toward and through the area, so 
too associated showers and storms. The strong to severe threat 
remains on the lower overall in the traditional, organized, sense 
for the area with supportive deep layer shear remaining displaced 
well north. There should be modest MUCAPE values ahead of the front 
later today, but the question becomes just when first storms may 
enter NW/N Missouri. Should the suggested slower frontal progression 
trend prevail, storms may not arrive until around/after 06z. This 
would tend to limit the severe threat as MUCAPE subsides and 
activity becomes elevated. Will note though that dry low-levels will 
be in place and evaporatively enhanced down drafts / downbursts 
could yet be possible with any of the more robust initial updrafts. 
Generally expect more a general shower / isolated thunder threat at 
the moment though. No issues with the new SPC Day 1 Marginal Risk 
over the far NW/N.

Into Wednesday, frontal progress is the key. Aside from the already 
discussed heat, it too would dictate location of any strong/severe 
storm threats Wednesday afternoon/evening. The new SPC Day 2 Outlook 
has expanded the Marginal Risk northward vs the old Day 3 Outlook, 
also suggesting a slower frontal passage trend. Overall, environment 
ahead of the front Wednesday will be similar to that on Tuesday, 
aside from being further south. At least modest MUCAPE >1500 J/kg is 
likely, but looks to continue to lack overall supportive deep layer 
shear. The resulting main risk would be strong and damaging winds 
given the dry low levels / inverted-V model soundings. There may be 
a small window for hail as well, dependent on just how much 
instability is able build in ahead of the front and if a bit better 
shear environment can develop. 

By Thursday, widespread relief behind the frontal passage, finally 
putting an end to the incessant heat discussions of late. Much 
welcome highs in the low to mid 80s across the entirety of the area. 
And 80s largely forecast through the weekend. The next opportunity 
for precipitation may move through Saturday as deterministic 
synoptic models depict another frontal boundary dropping through the 
Northern and Central Plains from a surface low lifting northward 
through Minnesota and into Ontario.
